Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the voltage from a Honeywell MICROpeL MP-741 combustible gas sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on the SPI bus using CE0, channel 0, with a 1 MHz SPI clock, operates in single‑ended mode, retries any ADC read failure after a 100 ms delay, prints the measured voltage and a placeholder PPM value to the console once per second, and appends a timestamp, voltage, and PPM to a file named gas_log.txt while checking for SPI initialization errors, SPI transfer failures, and file open errors; the program must install a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C triggers clean closure of the SPI interface and graceful termination of the driver library, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths, and it should run as a simulated propane leak detector until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the X, Y, and Z acceleration signals from an ADXL335 analog accelerometer using an MCP3008 10‑bit ADC on SPI mode 0, with the ADXL335 X‑out connected to MCP3008 channel 0, Y‑out to channel 1, and Z‑out to channel 2, the MCP3008 chip‑select tied to GPIO8 (BCM), MOSI to GPIO10 (BCM), MISO to GPIO9 (BCM), and SCLK to GPIO11 (BCM); the program must initialize the SPI bus and each channel, verify every initialization step and each SPI transaction, gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, apply a Kalman filter to the raw 10‑bit samples from each axis using the 3.3 V reference to produce smoothed acceleration values in g, print the filtered X, Y, and Z values to the console at a steady rate of 10 Hz, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads three Texas Instruments DRV5055VA Hall‑Effect sensors as digital logic states on individual GPIO pins (sensor 1 on GPIO4 BCM, sensor 2 on GPIO17 BCM, sensor 3 on GPIO27 BCM) every 100 milliseconds, simulates an ADC by interpreting HIGH as 3.3 V and LOW as 0.0 V, converts each state to a magnetic field strength value, and logs the three computed values in millitesla to a file named magnetic_log.txt in a comma‑separated line format “sensor1_mT,sensor2_mT,sensor3_mT”, flushing the file after each write; the program must include robust error handling for GPIO access and file I/O, printing a warning to stderr whenever any computed magnetic field falls outside the range –100 mT to +100 mT, skipping the logging for that iteration if any GPIO read fails, using only individual API call() operations for broad compatibility, and must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources properly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the soil moisture sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on the SPI bus (CE0, 500 kHz, mode 0) using channel 0 in single‑ended mode, evaluates the moisture level every 60 seconds, and drives a pump relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM, active‑high) so that the pump is turned on when the moisture reading falls below 30 % and turned off when it rises to 30 % or above, while logging every event—including program start, each pump on/off transition, any errors, and program termination with timestamps—to a file named “watering.log”, handling errors by checking all driver and SPI calls and logging any ADC read failures but continuing operation, and ensuring a clean shutdown by installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn the pump off before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads analog values from three single‑ended MCP3008 channels (0, 1, and 2) over the SPI bus /dev/spidev0.0 (SPI0, CE0, SPI_MODE_0, 8 bits per word, 1 MHz) and logs the readings once per second to a CSV file named sensor_data.csv, with each line containing the three channel values in order; the program must check the result of every open, ioctl, read, and write call and, on any failure, print an error message and exit gracefully, and it must also install a SIGINT handler so that when the user presses Ctrl +C the CSV file is properly closed and the SPI resources are released before the program terminates.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that subscribes over MQTT on TCP to mqtt.eclipseprojects.io:1883, listening on the topic “home/led_control” with client ID “rpi_led_control” and QoS 0, parses each incoming JSON payload expecting exactly the key “led_state” with a boolean value, rejects any other keys or types, and drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) as output, turning the LED off at startup, setting the pin HIGH when led_state is true and LOW when false; the program must implement robust error handling that logs all connection failures, JSON parsing errors, and protocol violations to stderr with timestamps, and uses an exponential reconnection backoff starting at 1 s, then 2 s, 4 s, and so on up to a maximum of 60 s; it must employ the provided MQTT client callbacks with a start/stop loop, use the supplied JSON parsing utility, and control the GPIO via the given driver API calls, while installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown that disconnects from MQTT, turns off the LED, and releases all driver resources, guaranteeing that every exit path—whether normal, error, or signal‑driven—leaves no resources allocated.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the digital output (DO) of a KY‑038 sound sensor module on a single‑bit GPIO bus, using the sensor’s DO pin connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), and prints the sound level reading (0 or 1) to the console each loop iteration with a 100 ms delay between reads; when the sensor reports a sound event—remembering that the KY‑038 DO pin goes LOW when the detected sound exceeds the onboard potentiometer threshold—the program must trigger an alarm LED attached to GPIO18 (BCM) by turning the LED on for 1 s and then off, and continue monitoring; the implementation must verify successful initialization of the GPIO driver, successful opening of the chip, successful line request, and must check the result of every I/O operation, handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully by printing an error message and exiting; finally, the program must catch SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) or SIGTERM and cleanly release all GPIO lines before exiting, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors the SW‑420 vibration sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) via the /dev/gpiochip0 GPIO character device, requesting the single line with the consumer label “vibration‑monitor” and configuring it for falling‑edge detection because the sensor’s DO output is active‑low, open‑collector (idle HIGH, pulls LOW when vibration exceeds the threshold). The program must robustly check every driver call (opening the chip, obtaining the line, requesting the event, waiting for an event, reading the event) and every file I/O call (opening /var/log/vibration_shutdown.log in append mode, writing with a timestamped line, and closing), reporting any failure with perror, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly; on each detected falling‑edge event the program should read the event using the single‑line event API, append a timestamped message to the log file and also print the same message to stdout, then invoke system("sudo shutdown -h now"); finally, on every exit path the code must release the GPIO line and close the chip to clean up all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that initializes the BMP280 barometric sensor on I2C bus 1 (SDA = GPIO2/pin 3, SCL = GPIO3/pin 5), first reads and verifies the sensor’s chip ID, then repeatedly reads raw pressure and temperature data every 5 seconds, applies the required compensation to compute altitude, and appends each computed altitude together with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named altitude_log.txt, flushing the file after every write; the program must handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor‑absent conditions, and file‑open failures by printing descriptive messages to stderr, and it must clean up all resources—including closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and terminating the driver—when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM, while always remembering that the BMP280 operates at 3.3 V logic and must never be driven with 5 V.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads an LM35 analog temperature sensor through an MCP3008 10‑bit ADC connected on SPI0 using chip‑enable CE0 and GPIO pins 8, 9, 10, 11, sampling the temperature every 5 seconds, storing each reading as a float in a circular buffer of 120 entries, printing each value to the console in the exact format “Temperature: XX.XX °C”, and after each sample overwriting the entire buffer to a binary file named temp_log.dat opened in mode wb+ so that the file always contains exactly 120 float values with the oldest data replaced when the buffer wraps; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver, opening of the SPI device, and each SPI transfer, printing an error and skipping the current reading if a transfer fails while continuing operation, and if the file cannot be opened it must print an error and continue without file logging; finally, it must install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the SPI interface, terminate the driver cleanly, and exit gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the ambient light from a BH1750 I2C light sensor on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) and the sound level from a MAX4466 analog microphone connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC accessed via the SPI bus (/dev/spidev0.0), samples both sensors once per second, and appends each reading to a file named environmental_log.txt using the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Light: [lux], Sound: [raw ADC value]”, while handling any I2C or SPI communication errors and sensor‑absent conditions without crashing, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released and the program terminates gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM, all without using any existing driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads the digital output of a Keyes KY‑026 flame sensor module connected to the GPIO bus as a digital input on BCM pin 17, initializing the line for input with a pull‑down resistor, then polls the pin once every second, logging each reading to a CSV file named flame_events.log with columns timestamp, pin and state, and printing an alarm message to stdout whenever the sensor reports a HIGH (active HIGH on flame); the program must check the result of every driver library API call (the library’s API call*, the library’s API call*) and on any failure print an error message to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status, and it must clean up all GPIO resources both on normal termination and when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the TMP36 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC using the SPI bus with chip‑enable CE0 at a 500 kHz clock, converts the raw ADC value to degrees Celsius, and then drives an MCP4725 DAC on the I2C bus to output a voltage proportional to the measured temperature; the program must sample every 0.5 seconds, log each reading to a file named temperature_log.txt with a timestamp, the raw ADC count, the calculated temperature in °C, and the DAC voltage, also echoing the same information to stdout, and must include robust error handling that checks all initializations, SPI transfers, I2C writes, and file operations, gracefully handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions with retries and clear error messages, and must perform a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT by closing the SPI interface, the I2C interface, the log file, and terminating any driver resources, while adhering to the constraint of not using any driver library or deprecated APIs.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads moisture from three DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 analog resistive sensors connected to an MCP3008 ADC via the SPI bus on CE0, mode 0 at 1 MHz, with the sensors wired to MCP3008 channels 0, 1, and 2, then sleeps for 60 seconds between cycles, appends each reading to a file named soil_data.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” with one line per sensor per cycle, prints an error and exits with code 1 if any of the required driver functions fail, prints an error and continues if an ADC value is invalid, and on receipt of SIGINT closes the SPI interface, closes the log file, terminates the driver, and prints a goodbye message, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths while using only the provided driver functions.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that sequentially activates and deactivates four Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relay modules connected as a light sequencer on the GPIO digital output bus, using BCM pins 17, 22, 23, and 24 for relays 1‑4 respectively; the program must initially set all relay pins to inactive (LOW, assuming active‑high relays), then in an infinite loop activate each relay for one second, deactivate it, wait one second before moving to the next relay, and repeat this pattern indefinitely, while checking the result of every driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, etc.) for errors, providing clear comments throughout, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that, on exit, deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines; no SPI, ADC, temperature sensor, or logging functionality may be used and only standard C libraries together with the driver library may be employed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the analog output of a Keyes KY-038 sound sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over the SPI bus CE0 on GPIO 8 using mode 0 at 1 MHz, sampling every 10 ms, and when the measured value exceeds a defined threshold it must turn on an LED wired to GPIO 16 (BCM) for 500 ms, log the event with a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” to a file named sound_events.log, apply a debounce delay after each trigger, and gracefully handle any SPI transfer failures, invalid ADC channel selections, or GPIO initialization errors by checking all driver library calls and file operations; the program must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt cleanly releases resources by closing the SPI interface, terminating the driver library, and turning off the LED, and it must be written using the driver library, not the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the analog output of a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor through an MCP3008 on SPI channel 0 configured at 1 MHz mode 0, polls the sensor once per second, appends the rain level together with a timestamp to a file named rain_log.txt (flushing after each write), and based on a default rain‑threshold value of 5 decides whether to close or open a window: when the measured level exceeds the threshold the program must drive a motor forward for exactly three seconds using the L298N‑based DC motor driver with IN1 connected to GPIO17 (BCM), IN2 to GPIO18 (BCM) and ENA (PWM) to GPIO27 (BCM) at a PWM duty of 150 within a range of 255, otherwise it must drive the motor in reverse for three seconds; the window is assumed initially open; the code must check every initialization, system call and I/O return value, handling failures to initialize the driver library, open the SPI device or the log file by printing clear error messages and performing proper cleanup, and must also detect and log any SPI transfer or file‑write errors without crashing; signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM must set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag that causes the main loop to stop the motor, close the SPI interface, close the log file and terminate the driver library before exiting, and all resources must be released on any exit path; the program should be compiled with gcc -o rain rain.c -lthe driver library -lrt -lpthread.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors the analog output of a MAX9814 electret microphone amplifier with automatic gain control using a bit‑banged ADC sampling on BCM GPIO26, detects a clap event, and when a valid clap is recognized (respecting a 50 ms debounce interval) turns on an LED connected to BCM GPIO16 for 500 ms while printing a timestamped detection message to the console; the implementation must verify that the ADC driver and GPIO mode settings are successfully initialized, handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and include a SIGINT handler that, on Ctrl + C, turns off the LED and cleanly releases all resources, all written in C11 without using any deprecated APIs and running until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads the Sharp GP2Y0A21YK0F IR distance sensor, which for this exercise is connected as a digital input on GPIO17 (BCM) via the GPIO digital input bus, treating the analog output as a binary 0 or 1 value; the program must log each read to a file named distance_log.txt in append mode with a timestamp formatted as YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, print “Feeder Activated” to the console when the sensed distance is less than 200 mm and “Feeder Idle” otherwise, handle any errors opening or reading the GPIO file by printing an error message and retrying after a one‑second delay, retry after one second on any other error, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the program cleanly unexports GPIO17 and exits, running indefinitely until interrupted while noting that a real implementation would require an ADC such as an MCP3008 but the current requirement treats the sensor as a digital input.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the Vegetronix VH400 soil moisture sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on the SPI bus (CE0, SCLK = GPIO11, MOSI = GPIO10, MISO = GPIO9) using single‑ended channel 0, samples the moisture level every 60 seconds, converts the ADC value to a moisture percentage, and activates a 12 V submersible water pump connected to a relay on GPIO17 (BCM) when the percentage falls below a defined threshold, logging each sample to a file named soil_moisture.log with a timestamp, the moisture percentage, and the pump status (ON or OFF); the program must verify successful initialization of the SPI interface, the ADC, and the log file, handle sensor read failures gracefully, validate ADC readings, and on receipt of SIGINT perform a graceful shutdown that turns the pump off, closes the log file, and releases all GPIO resources, while respecting the constraint that the relay is active‑high and no external driver library or similar software component is used, relying only on modern APIs provided by the system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the DRV5055‑A1 Hall‑effect sensor through an external MCP3008 ADC over the SPI bus /dev/spidev0.0 configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, sampling the sensor voltage on MCP3008 channel 0 every 500 ms, converting the raw integer reading to magnetic field strength using integer arithmetic and printing the result with two decimal places, and appending a CSV line “<unix_epoch>,<B_mt_two_decimals>” to a file named magnetic_log.txt; the MCP3008 VDD and VREF must be tied to the 3.3 V rail, its DOUT line to GPIO10 (BCM), DIN to GPIO9 (BCM), CLK to GPIO11 (BCM), and CS/SHDN to GPIO8 (gpiochip0 line 8) (BCM), while the DRV5055‑A1 VCC is also powered from 3.3 V and its VOUT is connected to the ADC channel 0, and the program must include standard headers such as stdint.h, check the return value of every open, ioctl, SPI transfer, fopen and fprintf call propagating errors, log any ADC read failure to stderr, skip that sample and continue, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing the GPIO line, closing the SPI file descriptor, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the analog output of a TI DRV5055VA Hall‑effect sensor through an MCP3008 ADC connected on SPI0 CE0 using the SPI pins GPIO8, GPIO9, GPIO10 and GPIO11, samples the value on channel 0 every 100 ms, converts it to magnetic field strength, appends a timestamped reading to a file named magnetic_log.txt, and when the measured field exceeds a threshold of 10.0 mT turns on an LED wired to BCM GPIO21, turning it off otherwise; the program must verify that the SPI interface opens successfully, that each ADC read returns valid data, and that the log file can be opened, handling any initialization failures appropriately, and must install a SIGINT handler that performs graceful cleanup by closing the SPI connection, switching off the LED, and terminating the driver library before exiting, while using only the driver library for hardware access and performing real ADC reads rather than simulated values.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors soil moisture using a DFRobot resistive soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC on SPI channel 0, chip‑enable 0, mode 0 at 1 MHz, with the sensor wired to MCP3008 channel 0, reading the raw ADC value every 60 seconds and appending each reading to a file named moisture_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS <raw‑value>”, while any read failure must be recorded as an error line with the same timestamp and a value of –1; the implementation must include robust error checking for all initialization, system calls and I/O operations, handle SIGINT by cleanly closing the SPI interface, terminating any driver usage, releasing all resources and exiting, and must run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the analog‑output Melexis MLX91209 current sensor (0‑5 V range, ~100 mV/A typical) through an MCP3008 ADC connected on the SPI bus /dev/spidev0.0, with the sensor’s power‑enable line tied to GPIO17 (BCM numbering) and the sensor’s voltage output wired to MCP3008 channel 0, sampling the current once every second, converting the ADC reading to amperes, and appending a line to a CSV file named current_log.txt in the format “timestamp,current_A”; the program must verify that each initialization step—opening the SPI device, configuring the GPIO line, and opening the log file—succeeds, must detect and handle sensor‑absent or communication failures without crashing, and must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown that releases the GPIO line, closes the SPI device, and closes the log file, while explicitly avoiding the use of any driver library for GPIO or the ADC.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the analog‑output Melexis MLX91211 current sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on hardware SPI0 (MCP3008 CE0 on GPIO8, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, SCLK on GPIO11, VDD/VREF tied to the Pi 5 V rail, MLX91211 VDD also on the Pi 5 V pin, and the sensor output connected to MCP3008 channel 0), configures the SPI bus to 1 MHz mode 0, samples the sensor every 100 ms using the library's API call(100000), converts the ADC reading to a current value, and appends a line to a file named current_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS XX.XX A” flushing after each write; the program must handle errors by printing an error message and exiting with a non‑zero status if the library's API call fails, terminating the driver library and exiting non‑zero on a second library's API call failure, printing a diagnostic and skipping the sample on any SPI transfer error, printing a warning and skipping the sample if the measured voltage is outside 0‑5 V, and on file‑open failure closing the SPI, terminating the driver library, and exiting non‑zero; a SIGINT handler should set a volatile flag to break the sampling loop cleanly, and on normal or forced exit the code must close the log file, the library's API call, and the library's API call, include required headers such as unistd.h, and contain clear comments while using only the driver library's API functions and no nonexistent helpers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that monitors two Omron B5W-DB01 diffuse reflective proximity sensors connected via GPIO, with sensor 1 on GPIO4 (BCM) and sensor 2 on GPIO17 (BCM), each providing a single active‑low open‑collector digital output with an internal pull‑up, and implements a debounce routine that reads each sensor five times spaced 2 ms apart and uses the majority value, logs the state once per second to the console as “0” for object present and “1” for no object, prints “ALERT: Both sensors detect object” when both sensors report object presence simultaneously, checks the return status of every API call and exits with a clear error message on failure, and installs a SIGINT handler that releases all GPIO resources on termination, while respecting the constraint that the B5W-DB01 has no analog output and that no driver, library, or deprecated code may be used.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads soil moisture from a YL‑69 soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC on SPI channel 0, CE0, operating at a 1 MHz baud rate, with the sensor wired to MCP3008 channel 0; the program must sample every 60 seconds, convert the raw ADC value (expected between 300 and 800) to a moisture percentage using a calculate_moisture_level function, and log each reading with a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,moisture_percentage” to a file named soil_moisture_log.csv as well as print the same line to the console, while handling errors by checking driver library initialization, SPI open, SPI transfer, and file open, printing an error and retrying after a delay on SPI transfer failure without exiting, printing an error and continuing on file open failure, and ensuring proper cleanup on SIGINT by using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag in a signal_handler that closes the SPI handle, terminates the driver library, and exits cleanly, with all resources released on error paths such as terminating the driver library before returning if SPI open fails; the source must include the headers driver library.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, unistd.h, time.h, signal.h, string.h, define the constants SPI_CHANNEL(0), SPI_BAUD(1000000), MCP3008_CHANNEL(0), READ_DELAY(60), MIN_ADC(300), MAX_ADC(800), LOG_FILE("soil_moisture_log.csv"), and implement the functions read_mcp3008(int channel), calculate_moisture_level(int adc_value), log_data(double moisture_level), signal_handler(int signal), and spi_setup(spi_config_t config).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected on the GPIO bus with its output wired to GPIO17 (BCM) configured as an input with a pull‑down resistor, polling the pin every 50 ms and applying a 200 ms debounce delay after any state change followed by a re‑read to confirm motion, then upon confirmed motion triggers a camera snapshot saved as a JPEG with a filename containing the documented value and an ISO 8601 timestamp in the directory /home/pi/security_cam/; the program must initialize the driver, verify that initialization succeeded, construct the output path safely with snprintf, ensure the target directory exists before attempting capture, launch libcamera‑still using fork and execvp (never system()), check the child’s exit status and treat any non‑zero result as a capture error, log all key events—including startup, motion detection, capture success or failure, and shutdown—to syslog, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a clean shutdown by stopping the main loop, releasing driver resources, and closing syslog.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that captures grayscale images from an Arducam OV5647 CSI camera module using the CSI bus device supplied as a command‑line argument (default /dev/video0), configures the camera for an 8‑bit grayscale format, sets up memory‑mapped streaming with a single buffer, and then continuously dequeues frames, handling the EAGAIN condition by using select() with a 2‑second timeout, saving each frame as a sequential .pgm file named image_0001.pgm, image_0002.pgm, and so on; the program must include robust error handling for every open(), ioctl(), mmap(), fwrite(), and close() call, printing strerror(errno) on failure, must gracefully handle EAGAIN when dequeuing buffers, must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, and must install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that stop streaming and safely unmap the buffers, while never using the C++ API of libcamera.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that captures an MJPEG video stream from a USB webcam attached as /dev/video0, uses memory‑mapped buffers to retrieve each frame, monitors the device asynchronously with select() to avoid indefinite blocking, and writes a line containing the timestamp of every captured frame in the form “seconds.microseconds” to a file named frame_log.txt; the implementation must include robust error handling for every driver ioctl, all file operations, and the memory‑mapping steps, must release all resources cleanly on every exit path, and must support a graceful shutdown when a SIGINT is received, while strictly adhering to the documented MJPEG format and avoiding any use of external video‑capture libraries.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using the board’s GPIO software PWM bus and four active‑low push‑buttons with internal pull‑ups, where the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), the tilt‑up button to GPIO6 (BCM), the tilt‑down button to GPIO7 (BCM), the pan‑left button to GPIO8 (BCM) and the pan‑right button to GPIO9 (BCM); the program must generate a 50 Hz PWM period (20 ms) with pulse widths ranging from 1 ms to 2 ms (corresponding to duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000), initialize both servos to the mid‑position value 75, and on each button press adjust the corresponding axis by ±5 while clamping the position to the range 25–125, poll the button states every 50 ms, check the return status of every driver call and handle any request failures, and on receipt of SIGINT cleanly release all allocated resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running Bookworm 64‑bit that opens the USB camera on /dev/video0, uses select() with a 2‑second timeout to wait for a frame, requests buffers, memory‑maps them, queues a buffer, starts streaming, dequeues the captured frame, stops streaming, unmaps the buffers, frees them and closes the file descriptor, handling SIGINT so that all these steps are performed cleanly on interruption; the captured image, originally in the documented YUYV format, must be converted to RGB24, processed with a blur filter, then encoded as a JPEG file named capture_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg with quality set to 75, and every system call and memory allocation must be checked for failure with error messages printed to stderr and all resources released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running a 32‑bit or 64‑bit kernel with the V4L2 subsystem active that opens the CSI camera device node /dev/video0, checks that the node exists and can be opened, queries the device capabilities with VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, enumerates all supported frame sizes using VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES and for each size enumerates the available frame intervals with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS, then queries the V4L2_CID_FOCUS_AUTO control with VIDIOC_QUERYCTRL to determine whether autofocus is supported, printing a clear, human‑readable summary of the resolutions, frame rates and autofocus capability to stdout; the program must verify every ioctl return value, handle the cases where the device node is missing, cannot be opened, the camera does not support frame‑size or interval enumeration, or the focus control is absent, and exit with a non‑zero status on any fatal error.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using two hobby servos driven over the GPIO hardware PWM bus, with four active‑low push‑buttons wired to ground and using the internal pull‑up resistors; the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), while the UP, DOWN, LEFT and RIGHT buttons are on GPIO6, GPIO7, GPIO8 and GPIO9 respectively, all using 50 Hz PWM where each loop iteration increments the pulse width by 10 µs and the loop delays 50 ms, the pulse widths must be clamped between 1000 µs (minimum) and 2000 µs (maximum) with a center position of 1500 µs, the program must initialize the driver library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if initialization fails, output a startup message showing the pin assignments and the center position, respond to button presses by adjusting the appropriate servo pulse width in the allowed range, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops PWM on both servo pins using the library's API call, calls the library's API call() to release resources, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected on the GPIO bus with its output tied to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11), debounces each motion detection for two seconds, and otherwise polls the pin every 100 ms; when motion is detected the program must capture a JPEG snapshot from the Camera Module v2 at quality 85, store the file in a directory named motion_captures (creating the directory if necessary and handling an existing directory gracefully), then compose a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number and POST this payload together with the image to an HTTP endpoint at http://<IP>:<port>/upload, where the IP address and port are supplied as command‑line arguments; the program must initialize the sensor driver and the HTTP library, configure GPIO17 as an input with a pull‑down resistor, check and report any initialization, system call, file, or network errors to stderr, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a clean shutdown by releasing the driver, performing the required global cleanup of the HTTP library, and exiting, while ensuring the global HTTP library initialization is called exactly once at startup and the corresponding cleanup is called exactly once at exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that monitors the HC‑SR501 PIR sensor on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s output connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) as an input with edge‑falling detection, implements a 50 ms debounce by waiting for a falling edge with a timeout, and upon a valid motion event invokes the camera capture utility with the options ‑o <filename> ‑‑width 640 ‑‑height 480 ‑q 85 ‑‑timeout 2000 ‑‑nopreview to produce a timestamped JPEG saved in /home/pi/images using the filename format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg; each capture and any error from the capture command must be logged with a timestamp to /home/pi/motion_capture.log; the program must open the GPIO chip, claim GPIO17 as an input with edge‑falling (or edge‑rising) detection, check return codes of the capture command and log failures, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all driver library resources and closing file descriptors, while assuming the images directory already exists and avoiding any network publishing, ZeroMQ, or use of a driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32‑bit or 64‑bit) that opens the USB UVC camera on /dev/video0, uses VIDIOC_QUERYCAP to verify the device, configures the capture to the documented V4L2_PIX_FMT_YUYV with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, requests a single memory‑mapped buffer, starts streaming, and then uses select() with a 2‑second timeout (retrying ioctl calls on EINTR) to wait for a frame; after a successful capture it must check that the returned width, height and pixel format match the requested values before processing, copy the complete YUYV macroblocks (Y0,U,Y1,V) to avoid color corruption, crop a 200 × 150 region, and write exactly 200*150*2 bytes to a file named cropped.yuv, checking the return value of every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen and fwrite and printing any errno with perror followed by EXIT_FAILURE on error; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must cleanly stop streaming, unmap the buffer, close the file descriptor and free any allocated memory.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads arrow‑key presses and a ‘q’ character from stdin, uses the GPIO hardware PWM bus to drive two SG90 servo motors—one pan servo attached to GPIO17 (BCM) and one tilt servo attached to GPIO18 (BCM)—operating at a 50 Hz frequency, initializing the driver library and exiting with code 1 after printing an error if initialization fails, starting both servos at a neutral 90‑degree position, moving each servo in 5‑degree steps in response to the appropriate arrow key while enforcing angle limits of 0 to 180 degrees and printing clear error messages for any out‑of‑range angle or PWM failure, inserting a 100 ms delay between successive commands, and handling cleanup by setting both servos to neutral, terminating the driver library cleanly, and exiting when a SIGINT signal is received or the user presses ‘q’.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and parses the CPU usage percentage from /proc/stat, then renders both values once per second on an SSD1306 128×64 I2C OLED display attached to I2C bus 1, using a basic 5×7 bitmap font for text; the program must check every I2C write operation for errors, handle file‑read failures by returning specific error strings to be shown on the OLED, log any I2C communication failures to stderr and exit gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler to cleanly release all resources before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the pulse output of a YF‑S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), computes the instantaneous flow rate and accumulates total volume, logs the current flow rate and total volume to the console once every second, and updates an HD44780 LCD attached via I2C bus 1 every ten seconds to display the same current flow rate and accumulated volume; the implementation must include robust error handling for any failures during GPIO initialization and must anticipate and manage possible I2C communication errors, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO and I2C resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads an anemometer pulse on GPIO17 (BCM) using an interrupt on the rising edge, counts pulses over a 500 ms sample window to compute real‑time wind speed, and reads wind direction from a wind vane connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0/CE0 in mode 0 at 1 MHz; the program must then update a 16x2 LCD with a PCF8574 backpack on I2C bus 1 to display both wind speed and direction every 500 ms, checking the result of every driver library, I2C and SPI call, detecting sensor‑absent conditions such as the ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023 or any I2C/SPI failures and printing diagnostic messages to stderr while continuing to run, and finally handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the SPI handle, the I2C handle and any driver library resources, using the provided driver library’s I2C and SPI bit‑bang helpers or direct /dev/i2c and /dev/spidev access via its spi0SPIOpen call where appropriate.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that measures water flow rate using a single YF‑S201 water flow sensor whose pulse output is connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) and displays the result on an LCD1602 attached via I2C bus 1; the program must count sensor pulses over a 1‑second interval to compute the flow in liters per minute and show “Flow Rate:” on the first line of the LCD and the calculated value formatted as “X.XX L/min” on the second line, while providing robust error handling for driver library initialization, GPIO mode and alert setup, and any I2C bus open or write failures, also detecting and handling sensor‑absent conditions such as zero pulses for extended periods, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path and perform a graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that drives an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix over the GPIO bus, using the row anodes on GPIO 17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM) and the column cathodes on GPIO 5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20 (BCM), scanning each row with an 800 µs delay, lighting an LED by setting the corresponding row HIGH and column LOW, and rendering two wave‑like animations that shift each frame, one moving left‑to‑right and the other right‑to‑left; the program must check every driver call, print descriptive error messages to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status on failure, and must handle a graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing all GPIO lines and performing cleanup, while adhering to the constraint of not using any driver library or deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that creates a wave‑like animation on an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix driven directly over GPIO, with the row anodes connected to GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 (BCM) and the column cathodes to GPIO 14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 (BCM); the program must scan the columns left to right, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW, then for each column set the column cathode LOW and light the LEDs sequentially by setting the corresponding row anodes HIGH, observing a 150 ms delay between columns, checking the result of every GPIO operation and handling a chip‑open failure, using the driver library v2 API for all GPIO calls, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly releases all GPIO lines on exit, while respecting the hardware constraint that each column cathode is wired through a current‑limiting resistor (e.g., 220 Ω) and that a column lights when its cathode is LOW and all row anodes are HIGH, and the program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance measurements for multiple targets from an STMicroelectronics VL53L3CX Time‑of‑Flight multi‑target sensor connected on I2C bus 1, polling the sensor every 100 ms and printing to the console ISO‑8601 timestamped distance values for all detected targets; the program must verify the sensor model ID during initialization, perform the required complex proprietary initialization sequence (or clearly stub the proprietary firmware download with a descriptive comment while keeping the I2C communication and error handling fully implemented), check every I2C read/write return code and handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads distance data from a Melexis MLX75031 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and appends each reading to a file named depth_log.csv, creating a CSV header row if the file is newly created and writing timestamped distance values; the program must verify successful initialization of the sensor interface, opening of the I2C bus, each I2C read/write transaction, and all file operations, and if an I2C read fails it must log a row with distance ‑1, attempt to re‑open the I2C handle, and continue sampling, while also handling SIGINT to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates the sensor interface without using any driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads proximity and ambient‑light data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 proximity/ambient‑light sensor attached to I2C bus 1, sampling every 500 ms, and appends each reading to a file named biometric_log.txt prefixed with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; the program must handle I2C read failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing, and if the sensor is absent or initialization fails it must print a diagnostic message to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status, while also installing a SIGINT handler that, upon receipt, cleanly closes the I2C handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls the sensor’s library API call() before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously polls an E18‑D50NK IR proximity sensor connected to GPIO line 4 (BCM, physical pin 7) every 100 ms, reads the sensor which drives the line LOW when an object is within the calibrated range and HIGH otherwise, and detects the falling edge from HIGH to LOW so that a timestamped entry is written only once per detection to a file named proximity.log using an ISO 8601 UTC format such as “2024-01-15T12:34:56Z Object detected”; when a detection occurs the program must also blink an LED attached to GPIO line 17 (BCM, physical pin 11) by turning it on for 100 ms and then off, and it must check the return status of every driver call, handle any file‑I/O errors, and on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—release the GPIO lines and close the chip, opening the GPIO chip first with the library’s API call that takes the default chip name and, if that fails, falling back to the library’s API call with the string “the library’s API call”, never invoking the API without arguments.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads proximity and ambient light data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor attached to I2C bus 1, first verifying the sensor’s PART_ID before entering an infinite loop that samples the two measurements once per second, and logs each reading to a file named biometric_data.log in CSV format with an ISO‑8601 timestamp followed by the proximity value and the ambient light value, flushing the file after every write; the program must check the return code of every I2C read and write operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors in a graceful manner, and install a SIGINT handler that, upon termination, closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and calls the sensor’s API call() function for proper cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that drives an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor over GPIO, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the TRIGGER output and GPIO 27 (BCM) as the ECHO input, with a 1 kΩ/2 kΩ voltage divider on the echo line to protect the 3.3 V‑tolerant pins from the sensor’s 5 V logic; the program must issue a 10 µs trigger pulse, then wait up to 30 ms for the echo rise and up to another 30 ms for the echo pulse width, compute the distance, reject any reading outside the 2‑400 cm range, and every 60 seconds log the result to a file named distance_log.txt with an ISO‑8601 timestamp, including explicit error or timeout entries, and if the measured distance is below 15 cm also log the message “Time to water the plant!”; all driver calls must be checked for failure, handling the sensor‑absent case where the echo never rises and the timeout case where the echo stays high, and the application must catch SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all resources and closes the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the distance from a TDK InvenSense ICU‑20201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, sampling every 100 ms, and drives an LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) such that the LED is turned on when the measured distance is below 20 cm and off otherwise, while logging each distance reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt; the implementation must check the result of every I2C, driver library, and file operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors in a graceful manner, and ensure that all resources—including the I2C handle, the GPIO pin, and any driver state—are cleanly released on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads proximity and ambient light data from a Silicon Labs Si1182‑GMR Optical Proximity and Ambient Light Sensor on I2C bus 1, sampling both measurements every 500 ms, and appends each reading with a timestamp to a file named biometric_log.txt; the implementation must check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, retry any failed read up to three times, and gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, while also installing a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) handler that cleanly releases the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates any driver resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads distance measurements from a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at a 50 ms polling interval, lights an LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) whenever the measured distance falls below a configurable threshold (default 100 mm, supplied as the first command‑line argument), logs each reading with a timestamp to a file named “tof_log.txt”, verifies the sensor’s WHO_AM_I register during initialization, checks all I2C read/write return codes, gracefully handles sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions without crashing, and ensures that on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT—the program releases the I2C handle, resets the GPIO, and performs any required driver cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that communicates with an Omron B5L‑LD50‑07050 3D TOF sensor over the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) to detect intrusion events within 1 meter and log the average distance; the program must send the documented 4‑byte command frame to request a measurement, wait at least 10 ms before reading the documented 15‑byte response, verify that byte 0 matches the documented header value, extract the 16‑bit big‑endian distance from bytes 11 and 12, sample the sensor ten times per cycle with a 100 ms delay between cycles, compute the average distance, and when the average is less than 1000 mm write a timestamp and the average distance to a file named intrusion_log.txt; all I2C open, ioctl, read and write calls must be checked for failure, and the code must gracefully handle sensor‑absent (I2C NACK) and bus‑error conditions, while also installing a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl‑C closes the I2C file descriptor and any open log files and releases all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to periodically read the distance from an Adafruit VL53L0X Time‑of‑Flight sensor, verifying the sensor’s presence at startup by reading its model ID register and confirming it matches the documented value, and exiting cleanly with an error message if the read fails or the ID mismatches; after successful initialization the program must poll the RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS with roughly a 100 ms timeout, obtain a distance measurement, and every 500 ms print to stdout a line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS Distance: <N> mm”, while checking every I2C call for errors and printing strerror(errno) on failure, issuing a warning to stderr and continuing to the next iteration for any read/write error that occurs during the loop; the program must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by closing the I2C handle, invoking the library’s cleanup call, and exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the 16‑bit proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 optical sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 SDA / GPIO3 SCL) and logs the values to the console every 500 ms, while checking each driver library or I2C call for errors, detecting a sensor‑absent condition by a NACK on the initial write, handling any bus errors gracefully without crashing, and installing a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C cleanly closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s API call() for proper cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads the Texas Instruments OPT3101 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, logging every 500 ms the distance measurement from channel 0, the ambient light value, and any error flags to the console, while implementing robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as a missing sensor or bus errors and guaranteeing that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the trigger output and GPIO 18 (BCM) as the echo input, issuing a 10 µs trigger pulse each cycle, waiting up to 200 ms for the echo rising edge and up to 200 ms for the echo falling edge, and performing one read per second; each valid measurement must be logged to the console together with a timestamp, while the code must handle driver library initialization failure, echo‑edge timeouts, and invalid pulse durations (≤ 0 µs or > 38 ms, the HC‑SR04 maximum range timeout), include a comment noting that the HC‑SR04 operates at 5 V and the Pi GPIO is only 3.3 V tolerant and therefore a 1 kΩ resistor must be used on the echo line within the library’s API call() that provides microsecond precision, and finally ensure graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by invoking the library’s API call() on all exit paths.

/*
 * ADPD105 CCT Logger for Raspberry Pi Zero W
 *
 * Reads two ADPD105 photometric front-end sensors on the I2C bus
 * (typically /dev/i2c-1) and computes the average correlated color
 * temperature (CCT) from the sensor data.  The results are logged
 * once per second to cct_log.csv.
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   ADPD105 #1 SDA -> GPIO2 (pin 3)
 *   ADPD105 #1 SCL -> GPIO3 (pin 5)
 *   ADPD105 #1 VDD -> 3.3 V
 *   ADPD105 #1 GND -> GND
 *   ADPD105 #2 SDA -> GPIO2 (pin 3)
 *   ADPD105 #2 SCL -> GPIO3 (pin 5)
 *   ADPD105 #2 VDD -> 3.3 V
 *   ADPD105 #2 GND -> GND
 *
 * Build:
 *   gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o cct_logger cct_logger.c
 *
 * Run:
 *   ./cct_logger

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the absolute pressure and temperature from a Melexis MLX90824 absolute pressure sensor over the I2C bus, performing a read cycle every 2 seconds, and appends each measurement together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named pressure_log.txt; the program must check the result of every driver library or I2C call, and if the sensor is absent, the bus reports an error, or a read fails, it must log the error with a timestamp instead of silently skipping, and it must ensure that on all exit paths—including normal termination, SIGINT, and SIGTERM—it cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the sensor library’s cleanup API, while running indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the temperature from an STMicroelectronics LM75B sensor on the I2C bus once every second, stores the last 60 samples in a circular buffer in memory, computes the running average, and drives a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the fan is turned on when the average exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off when it falls below 26.0 °C; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, opening of the I2C interface, each I2C read, and each GPIO write, logging any failures to stderr and simply retrying on the next cycle without crashing, and it must handle SIGINT or SIGTERM by stopping the fan, closing the I2C handle, and terminating the driver library cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C, waiting 45 ms after issuing the first measurement command before reading, then sampling once every second, reading exactly nine bytes each cycle and validating each CRC using the Sensirion CRC‑8 polynomial and its documented initial value; the program must log each reading to a file named airflow.log in CSV format with columns timestamp, differential pressure (Pa) and temperature (°C), print a warning to stderr whenever the pressure exceeds 5.0 Pa, robustly handle I2C read/write failures, CRC mismatches and the case where the sensor is absent, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handle, close the log file and invoke the library’s call() cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from an STTS2004 temperature sensor on the I2C bus, logs the temperature to stdout once per second, and drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the LED is set high when the temperature exceeds 28 °C and low when it falls below 27 °C; the program must check the result of every I2C read and every GPIO operation, and on repeated I2C failures it must log the errno details and exit cleanly, while handling SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing all driver library resources, closing the I2C file descriptor, turning the LED off, and then exiting.
pinned_library: Linux i2c-dev for I2C access, libgpiod for GPIO/LED control

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 45 ms after initiating a measurement before reading the result, retrieving exactly nine bytes consisting of two bytes of differential pressure followed by a CRC byte, two bytes of temperature followed by a CRC byte, and three bytes of scale‑factor data, validating each CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial and initialization value, logging the measured values with timestamps to a file named flow_data.txt, handling any I2C communication errors or the sensor‑absent condition gracefully, and ensuring that all resources are released on every exit path by installing a signal handler for SIGINT that performs the required cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor on the I2C bus using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM, bus 1 default) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM, bus 1 default), waiting at least 20 ms after issuing a no‑hold command and sampling every 60 seconds, logging each reading to a file named environment.log in CSV format with columns timestamp, temperature_c, humidity_pct while also printing the same line to stdout, handling errors by retrying each I2C transaction up to three times, validating sensor presence at startup by reading its electronic ID or firmware revision and exiting with a non‑zero status after logging a timestamped error to both the log file and stderr if the sensor is absent, flushing the log after every write, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call, while using the “Measure Relative Humidity, No Master Hold” and “Measure Temperature, No Master Hold” commands or alternatively the “Read Temperature from Previous RH Measurement” command and performing raw byte transfers rather than register‑addressed reads.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a TI HDC1080 sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 20 ms after each trigger to allow conversion, and appends a line to enviro_log.txt every 5 seconds in the format “timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent”; the program must initialize the driver and open the I2C bus with error checking, gracefully handle any I2C communication failures or a missing sensor by skipping the log entry on error, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handle and terminate the driver, running in an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the temperature from a Sensirion STS40 I2C temperature sensor on the I2C bus, waiting 10 ms after each trigger for the conversion to complete and sampling the value every 5 seconds, logging each reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named temperature_log.txt; the program must open the I2C device with open(), set the slave address using ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read exactly three bytes (two data bytes and one CRC8 byte), verify the CRC8 using the Sensirion‑specified polynomial, and on any error condition—including failures to open the device, ioctl, read, write, CRC mismatch, or open the log file—print a descriptive message to stderr and then continue looping; it must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting, and run indefinitely in an infinite loop.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors air‑duct pressure in a simulated HVAC system using the Sensirion SDP810‑500Pa differential pressure sensor on the I2C bus, triggering a measurement, waiting at least 50 ms, then reading the 9‑byte result (2 bytes pressure, 1 byte CRC, 2 bytes temperature, 1 byte CRC, 3 bytes scale factor) once per second, validating every I2C read and write as well as each CRC‑8 using the polynomial and initial value documented for the sensor, logging each successful sample to a file named hvac_pressure_log.txt in CSV format with columns timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C, and on any I2C or CRC error writing an error line with the timestamp and continuing, checking the return of every initialization call (the two required library API calls and fopen) and exiting with an error message if any fails, and handling SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and calling the library’s cleanup API function before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that drives a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C, buffers CO₂, temperature and humidity readings in a thread‑safe circular buffer of capacity 100, and periodically persists the data to a timestamped CSV file in /var/log/scd40_data/ (creating the directory if it does not exist) with a header row, while logging any errors with timestamps to /var/log/scd40_error.log; the main loop must wait at least one second after issuing the start‑periodic‑measurement command before the first read, then read the sensor every five seconds, validating the CRC‑8 of each value using the polynomial and initial value documented for the device and, on any CRC failure or I2C read/write error, log the error and skip that reading; a separate logging thread must write the buffered records to the CSV file every sixty seconds, and the program must handle SIGINT by using a volatile sig_atomic_t running flag to stop the main loop, send the documented stop‑periodic‑measurement command, join the logging thread, flush any remaining buffered data to a final CSV file, close the I2C handle and cleanly terminate the driver without any resource leaks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 45 ms after each trigger for the measurement to complete and sampling once per second, reading the required nine bytes (two bytes of differential pressure followed by a CRC, two bytes of temperature followed by a CRC, and two bytes of scale factor followed by a CRC), validating each CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial and initial value, and logging each successful sample to a file named sdp810_log.txt in CSV format with columns timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C; the program must handle I2C open, write, and read errors as well as CRC failures by logging the error and continuing operation, and it must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt closes the I2C handle, terminates any driver resources, closes the log file, and exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads pressure and temperature from a TDK ICP-10110 pressure sensor on the I2C bus, initializing the driver library and opening the I2C bus with proper error checking, then in a loop triggered every 5 seconds waits 10 ms after each trigger before reading the sensor, appends each sample to a file named environmental_data.txt in append mode flushing after each write, prefixes each line with an ISO 8601 timestamp and also prints the reading to stdout, handling any I2C read/write errors by printing a message to stderr and skipping that sample, and installs a SIGINT handler that sets a flag to exit the loop, after which the program closes the I2C handle, closes the file, and calls the library’s cleanup API call().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the TDK ICP-10125 barometric pressure sensor over I2C, retrieving exactly six bytes per read (two pressure bytes, two temperature bytes, and two CRC bytes) while checking every I2C syscall for errors, handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and verifying the CRC on each sensor read; after each trigger a 20 ms delay must be observed, the sensor should be polled once per second, and the result used to drive a warning LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) where the LED blinks at 1 Hz (500 ms on, 500 ms off) under normal conditions and switches to a 5 Hz pattern (100 ms on, 100 ms off) whenever the measured pressure falls below 95 000 Pa, with the GPIO line requested, set to output, and toggled accordingly; the program must also install a SIGINT handler that safely closes the I2C file descriptor and releases the GPIO line before exiting.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient and object temperature from a Melexis MLX90614ESF-BAA infrared temperature sensor over the I2C bus, logs the timestamped readings to a file named temperature_log.txt every 2 seconds, and controls a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the fan turns on when the object temperature exceeds 30 °C and turns off when it falls below 28 °C; the program must validate driver library initialization, opening the I2C bus, and each I2C read/write operation, retrying any failed read up to three times with a 10 ms delay between attempts and skipping logging for invalid readings, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing the I2C handle, turning off the fan, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the Sensirion SHT40 sensor on I2C bus 1, issuing the measurement command, waiting at least 10 ms, then reading exactly six bytes, and streams the live temperature and humidity values to a local HTTP server on port 8080 using the library’s API call to serve an HTML page that displays the current temperature and humidity while clamping humidity to the range 0‑100 %; the implementation must include robust error handling for I2C communication such as sensor absence or bus errors with up to three retries per read, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals appropriately.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP102 on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, performs a measurement every 5 seconds, and appends each result to a timestamped CSV file named temperature_log.csv with lines formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,XX.XX”; the program must include standard headers such as errno.h and stdint.h to compile without warnings, check the success of all initialization and I/O calls, log any read failure to stderr while skipping that entry, and install a SIGINT handler so that when Ctrl+C is pressed the I2C handle is closed, the driver library is terminated, and the program exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC2010 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, polling the sensor’s MEASUREMENT_CONFIG register until bit 0 clears or a timeout of roughly 500 ms occurs, then outputs the readings to the console every five seconds; the implementation must check the result of every driver call, detect a missing sensor (NAK) and any bus‑error conditions, retry transient I2C failures only up to a defined maximum count, and include a clean shutdown triggered by Ctrl +C via a signal handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, closes the I2C handle, and invokes the library’s API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, waits approximately 45 ms for each measurement to complete, and logs to the console the raw 16‑bit pressure and temperature values every 500 ms; the program must open the I2C bus, verify that the driver library initializes correctly, check the result of every write and read operation, read exactly six bytes (two bytes pressure, one CRC, two bytes temperature, one CRC), validate each CRC‑8 checksum using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions gracefully, and on receipt of a SIGINT perform a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle and invoking the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4B that reads temperature from a TMP117, humidity from an AHT20, and motion detection from a PIR motion sensor, logging the values to daily timestamped CSV files with a header line “Timestamp,Temperature(C),Humidity(%),MotionDetected”; the TMP117 and AHT20 are connected on /dev/i2c-1, the PIR sensor is accessed via the library’s API call on line 17 and is wired to GPIO17 (gpiochip4 line 17, input), the program must sample every 1 second, retry I2C reads up to three times with a 10 ms backoff on failure, create a new log file at midnight each day, print a warning but continue if a sensor is not present at startup, handle I2C errors as described, and ensure all resources are cleanly released on every exit path including SIGINT and SIGTERM, building the code with gcc -o logger logger.c -lgpiod -lrt while using the documented I2C addresses for the TMP117 and AHT20.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors a YL‑83 rain sensor connected to GPIO17 (active‑low) via the GPIO bus, polling the sensor every 2 seconds, and when rain is detected commands an L298N motor driver to close a window by driving the motor forward for exactly 5 seconds using ENA on GPIO22, IN1 on GPIO23 and IN2 on GPIO24, then stops the motor; each detection, motor start, motor stop, and any error condition must be logged to stdout with a timestamp, the code must check the return status of every driver call and explicitly handle the situation where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and it must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers so that on program termination the motor is safely stopped and all GPIO lines are released, while deliberately excluding any DHT22 or humidity sensing functionality.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that modulates a common‑anode RGB LED connected on the GPIO bus with the red cathode on GPIO17, the green cathode on GPIO22, and the blue cathode on GPIO27, sampling the system every 500 ms to read the CPU load from /proc/stat by comparing successive samples and mapping the 0‑100 % load to a color gradient where 0 % is green (0,255,0), 50 % is yellow (255,255,0) and 100 % is red (255,0,0), using hardware PWM via the driver library to set PWM values clamped to 0‑255 for each channel, handling driver library initialization failures by printing an error to stderr and exiting with code 1, and installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn the LED off (all channels full off for a common‑anode LED) and cleanly invoke the library’s API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor on I2C‑1 (SDA = GPIO2/pin 3, SCL = GPIO3/pin 5) using the documented I2C address, waits for each measurement to complete before reading, and every 5 seconds formats the two values into a JSON string and transmits it via UDP to 192.168.1.100 on port 5000; the program must handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor‑absent conditions, and UDP send failures gracefully, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that cleanly release the I2C handle, close the UDP socket, and shut down the driver library on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that dynamically controls a PWM‑driven cooling fan based on temperature readings from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier connected on SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8); the fan PWM must be output on GPIO18 (BCM) using hardware PWM at 1 kHz with a duty range of 0‑255, the program shall read the temperature every 1 second, compute the duty cycle using a piecewise fan curve (0 % below 25 °C, linear ramp from 0 % to 50 % between 25 °C and 40 °C, steeper ramp from 50 % to 200 % between 40 °C and 60 °C, and 100 % above 60 °C), store each timestamp, temperature, and PWM duty cycle in a 20‑entry circular buffer, perform robust error checking for every the driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call); on any SPI transfer error or MAX31855 fault, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip the fan update for that cycle, initialize the driver library and open SPI channel 0 at 500 kHz mode 0, and on receipt of SIGINT stop the PWM, close the SPI interface, print the full contents of the circular buffer, terminate the driver library and then exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that communicates with a BMP180 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, configures GPIO2 as a falling‑edge interrupt with the internal pull‑up enabled, and toggles data logging each time the interrupt occurs; the main loop must poll at one‑second intervals, and when logging is active the program should read the sensor using oversampling setting OSS=3, verify that the calibration data is successfully read, obtain temperature in Celsius and pressure in Pascals, and append a line to an altitude_log.txt CSV file containing the timestamp, temperature, and pressure; every I2C read and write operation must be checked for errors, and the program must handle such errors gracefully, and on receipt of SIGINT it must close the I2C handle, close the log file, and release the GPIO before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads temperature from a MAX31865 RTD‑to‑digital converter over SPI0 using chip‑enable CE0 (GPIO8) at 1 MHz, operates the device in 3‑wire RTD mode with the bias voltage enabled, checks the fault status register on each read, computes the temperature using the Callendar‑Van Dusen equation, and logs the results every 5 seconds to a file named rtd_log.csv containing a timestamp and the temperature; the program must include robust error handling that logs SPI communication failures, sensor‑absent conditions, and any read errors without crashing, and it must perform a graceful shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by properly closing the SPI device file descriptor and the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature, humidity and pressure from a BME280 sensor attached to I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL, device file /dev/i2c-1) using the documented I2C address, verifies that the BME280 chip ID matches the documented value during initialization, and then logs a line to a file named bme280_log.csv every five seconds containing a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS”, the temperature in degrees Celsius, the relative humidity in percent, and the pressure in hectopascals; the program must check the result of every I2C read and write system call, handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and ensure that all file descriptors and file pointers are cleanly released on any exit path, including when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, employing the library's API call for I2C communication and the library's API call for a hardware timer that triggers every 50 ms; each reading must be stored in a circular buffer sized to hold timestamped pressure values for the last 60 seconds, from which a rolling average is computed, and if the current pressure deviates by more than 5 hPa from that average the program shall assert an active‑HIGH alert on GPIO24, logging the alert to stderr, while also logging any I2C failures or sensor absence with robust error handling; the sampling loop must use the library's API call for the 50 ms timer, and on receipt of SIGINT the program must cleanly release resources by closing the I2C interface, resetting GPIO24, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that configures I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 pressure sensor, validates the calibration data read from the documented registers before any measurement, and then uses a hardware timer interrupt to trigger a sample every 500 ms, reading temperature in degrees Celsius and pressure in pascals with the oversampling setting set to 0 (ultra low power) and appending the results to a file named bmp180_log.txt; the implementation must include robust error handling for all I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and must ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the CPU temperature from the thermal zone file /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, maps the temperature linearly to a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 25 kHz frequency and a 0‑255 range such that 40 °C corresponds to 0 % duty, 70 °C to 100 % duty and values are clamped below 40 °C and above 70 °C, drives a PWM‑controlled cooling fan accordingly, logs every 5 seconds to a file named fan_log.txt the current timestamp, temperature and duty cycle, and includes robust error handling for failures to read the temperature, write to the log file, or initialize the PWM driver, while also installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully stop the fan, close any open files and terminate the PWM driver before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA on GPIO2 pin 3, SCL on GPIO3 pin 5) using the documented default address when SDO is tied to GND and falling back to the documented alternative address, applies the Bosch 64‑bit compensation formulas, rewrites the ctrl_meas register in forced mode each loop to trigger a new measurement, and appends a line to weather_data.txt every five seconds in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa”, while checking every I/O call (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs) for errors, logging any sensor I/O failures to stderr and attempting to continue or exit gracefully, ensuring the sensor is powered from the 3.3 V rail only, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to break the logging loop, close the I2C file descriptor and any open files, and exit with status 0.
